name: Soccer (Association Football)
tagline: The world's game — one ball, two goals, and every culture on Earth playing it.
overview: Soccer — association football — is played between two teams of eleven who try to score by getting a ball into the other side's goal, using any part of the body except hands and arms. It is the simplest promise in sport: a ball, a field, two goals, and a rule that everyone plays by the same laws whether the match is in a World Cup final or a schoolyard.

No sport approaches its reach. FIFA counts more member associations than the United Nations has member states, and the World Cup final is the most-watched single sporting event on the planet. The game is Pakistan's street cricket, Brazil's Sunday carnival, and Europe's civic religion at once — which is why every other sport on earth eventually borrows its vocabulary: GOAT debates, transfer sagas, tactical pods.

Newcomers should know that the game rewards patience. Possession beats panic, and the first skill to learn is not shooting but the first touch — receiving the ball so your next action is already available. Everything else in this page builds on that one idea.
facts: 1863 — the Football Association (FA) in London wrote the Laws of the Game
FIFA (world, founded 1904); IFAB guards the Laws; six continental confederations
11 v 11 including a goalkeeper; variants from 3 to 9 a side
Two 45-minute halves plus stoppage time (about 100 minutes real time)
100-110 m by 64-75 m for full internationals; goals 7.32 m wide, 2.44 m high
Olympic sport for men since 1900, for women since 1996
211 FIFA member associations — more than any other sport's federation
history: Cuju in Han-dynasty China and countless folk footballs across Europe kick a ball for ritual, soldiers, and fun — without one agreed rulebook.
The Football Association meets in a London pub and separates 'football' from rugby's carrying game — the Laws of the Game are born.
The FA Cup (1871) and the Football League (1888) invent knockout and league football; professionalism is legalized in 1885.
FIFA forms in Paris; Uruguay hosts and wins the first World Cup in 1930 as the game goes global.
The European Cup (1955, now the Champions League) builds club football's world stage; the first Women's World Cup is held in 1991.
Olympic women's football arrives in 1996; VAR enters the World Cup in 2018 — the biggest Laws change in a generation.
formats: The full game: two 45-minute halves, the offside law, and the tactical depth that defines the sport.
Indoor 5-a-side with a smaller, heavier ball and walls out of play — the skill accelerator that shaped Messi and Ronaldo.
The recreational workhorse: smaller pitch, running substitutions, no offside in most leagues.
5-a-side on sand with acrobatic volleys and a three-period format — a FIFA-run world game of its own.
Over-50s phenomenon where running is banned — the sport's social heartbeat in later life.
skills: First touch
Killing an incoming ball so it lands a stride away, in the direction you want to go.
Partner throws or wall passes; trap with sole, inside, chest, thigh — 100 clean reps each before adding speed.
Passing
Pushing the ball with the inside of the foot: eyes up, ankle locked, follow through the target line.
Two-cone passing at 5, 10, 20 meters; then one-touch pairs. Accuracy target: 8 of 10 into a one-meter gate.
Dribbling
Ball on a string with small touches using laces and outside foot, head up between touches.
Cone slalom with both feet, then 1 v 1 games to small goals — the defender teaches what cones cannot.
Finishing
Striking with the instep (laces) for power, inside for placement; arriving at the ball, not waiting for it.
Start static at the penalty spot, then first-time finishes from crosses and cutbacks.
1 v 1 defending
Sideways-on jockeying, patience, and the tackle only when the touch is heavy.
Shadow defending in pairs; defender wins by delaying three seconds, not by stealing.
Aerial play
Timing jumps and heading with the forehead, eyes open — defense and attack in one skill.
Progress from self-toss headers to partner crosses; young players should start with lighter balls.
Goalkeeping
Set position, hand shape (W for high balls, scoop for ground), and the courage to arrive first.
Every drill ends with a save; add diving progression only on soft ground with a coach's eye.
rules: Eleven players a side, one of whom is a goalkeeper allowed to use hands only inside their own penalty area.
A match is two 45-minute halves; the referee adds stoppage time for injuries, substitutions, and delays.
Offside: at the moment a teammate plays you the ball, you cannot be beyond the second-last defender and involved in the play.
Direct free kicks punish kicking, tripping, pushing, and handball; an offense inside your own box gives a penalty kick.
Yellow card is a caution; two yellows or one red means you are sent off and your team plays a player short.
Restarts: throw-in when the ball crosses a touchline, goal kick or corner when it crosses a goal line.
Substitutions: most top competitions allow five per match from a bench of nine.
equipment: Size 5 (68-70 cm) for ages 13+; size 4 for younger players. A decent match ball runs $20-60.
Firm-ground studs for grass, turf shoes for artificial, indoor flats for futsal. $40-150 covers everything a beginner needs.
Mandatory in organized play — CE-marked, worn under the socks. $10-30.
Jersey, shorts, socks; numbered shirts entered the Laws in 1939. Club kits are optional; team colors are not.
Full-size 7.32 x 2.44 m; a folding 3 x 2 m goal turns any park into a training ground.
The cheapest performance upgrade in sport — a dozen cones enable half of every session plan.
training: Build the aerobic engine: players cover 10-12 km per match with 30-40 sprints, so long steady runs plus interval sessions are the base.
Lift with one leg at a time — split squats, single-leg RDLs — because soccer is a game of cutting and deceleration.
Protect knees and groins with Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks; both cut injury risk more than any gadget.
Touch comes from volume, not variety: 15 minutes of daily wall work beats an occasional fancy session.
Play small-sided games weekly; they multiply touches, decisions, and fitness in one drill.
pathway: School, park, and local club football — where almost every professional and every fan starts.
Professional clubs scout from age 8; structured coaching, trials, and league play three times a week.
U18 scholarship or college soccer; reserve teams and loan spells bridge to senior football.
Semi-professional regional leagues sit below the professional pyramid — the pyramid has dozens of rungs, not one.
National teams select from clubs; youth internationals (U17-U21) feed the full sides.
events: Every four years since 1930 — 48 teams from 2026; the most-watched sporting event on Earth.
Europe's club championship, midweek from autumn to a May final; the richest prize in club sport.
Every four years since 1991; the 2023 edition drew nearly two million spectators in Australia and New Zealand.
The Euros, Copa América, Africa Cup of Nations, and Asian Cup — each a World Cup in miniature.
Under-23 men's tournament with three over-age players; senior women's tournament since 1996.
legends: Brazil — the only player to win three World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970); the sport's first global superstar.
Argentina — carried the 1986 World Cup on his back, for better and for the Hand of God.
Argentina — eight Ballons d'Or and the 2022 World Cup; the dribbler who finished like a marksman.
Portugal — five Champions Leagues and the most international goals ever scored; longevity as a spectacle.
Brazil — six World Cups and the most World Cup goals of any player, man or woman; the women's game's first icon.
getting_started: Buy the boring essentials: one size-5 ball, shinguards, and firm-ground boots — under $100 all in.
Learn three touches first: inside-foot pass, sole-of-foot trap, outside-foot cut. Wall work for 15 minutes a day.
Join a pickup game or 5-a-side league within two weeks; the game teaches faster than drills alone ever will.
Watch one full match a week with intent — pick a single player and follow only them for 45 minutes.
Add two fitness sessions: one long run, one strength session with single-leg work.
Recruit friends for small-sided games; nothing in sport scales joy per dollar like a 5-a-side booking.
glossary: Nutmeg
Playing the ball through an opponent's legs — the game's smallest humiliation and greatest joy.
Hat-trick
Three goals by one player in one match; the match ball is theirs to keep.
Clean sheet
A goalkeeper or team conceding zero goals in a match.
Offside trap
Defenders stepping up in unison to catch attackers beyond the last line.
False nine
A centre-forward who drops into midfield, dragging defenders out of position.
Gegenpress
Winning the ball back within seconds of losing it — Klopp's signature and modern soccer's default.
Stoppage time
Added minutes at each half's end, at the referee's discretion.
Bicycle kick
An overhead volley struck mid-air, legs scissoring — soccer's signature acrobatic goal.
VAR
Video Assistant Referee — the 2018-introduced video review used for goals, penalties, red cards, and mistaken identity.
Tifo
The choreographed flags, mosaics, and banners supporters unveil at kickoff.
